{
    "id": "13-creative/brand-voice-development",
    "title": "Brand Voice Development",
    "category": "13-creative",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Define a reusable brand voice from values and audience, specifying tone dimensions, vocabulary rules, and example rewrites so all writers sound like one consistent speaker.",
    "body": "Brand Voice Development Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A brand voice is a small set of decisions applied consistently, not a mood board. The skill covers extracting voice traits from brand values, defining each trait as a position on a tone axis with do-and-never examples, writing vocabulary and punctuation rules, and validating drafts by rewriting the same sample in the defined voice. A voice is done when an unfamiliar writer can apply the spec and pass a blind consistency check. When to Use Use when an organization needs its writing to sound consistent across channels, writers, and formats, from support replies to marketing copy. Do not describe the voice only with adjectives such as friendly and bold. Without axis positions, vocabulary rules, and contrast examples, every writer interpolates differently. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Brand values, positioning, and audience definition | | | | No | Existing writing the voice should preserve or correct | | | | No | Channel-specific tone adjustments, keyed by channel | Procedure 1. Extract candidate voice traits from brand values and the audience relationship. 2. Reduce the traits to three to five axes and pick a position on each, with rationale. 3. Write do-and-never examples per trait so contrast is explicit, not implied. 4. Define vocabulary rules: preferred terms, banned terms, and grammar choices. 5. Rewrite one canonical sample passage in the new voice and annotate every change. 6. Run a blind consistency check with an unfamiliar writer before publishing the spec. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Trait axes, positions, and rules, machine-referenced per piece | | | | Before-and-after pairs demonstrating each trait | | | | Per-channel tone adjustments that preserve the traits | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Trait soup | Too many traits for writers to hold in mind | Cut to three to five axes | | Inconsistent across channels | One static tone applied everywhere | Define channel overrides that preserve traits | | Drift over time | No validation loop after the spec ships | Re-run consistency checks on live copy periodically | | Adjectives only | No axis positions or contrast examples | Require do-and-never pairs per trait | | Voice copies a competitor | Samples over-weighted toward external material | Anchor in the brand brief, not imitation | Security and Authority Boundary A voice spec encodes how an organization speaks and is a reputational asset. Keep positioning and unreleased campaign strategy confidential, and ensure the voice never overrides accuracy or legal disclosure requirements in regulated content. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Microsoft Writing Style Guide as a public voice and style reference (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/). 2. The Google developer documentation style guide (https://developers.google.com/style). {
    "id": "13-creative/character-design",
    "title": "Character Design",
    "category": "13-creative",
    "level": "basic",

    "description": "Build fictional characters as explicit profiles — voice, motivation, capability, limits — with mechanically checkable arc beats so characters stay consistent and their growth is deliberate.",
    "body": "Character Design Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A character is a contract with the reader: the way they speak, what they want, what they cannot do. Breaking that contract by convenience is how stories lose trust. This skill defines a character as a structured profile — identity, motivation, capabilities with explicit limits, and voice rules — plus a beat sheet for their arc, so consistency is checkable against a record instead of remembered vibes. When to Use Use when introducing a recurring character into any narrative work — prose, games, scripts — whose behavior must stay consistent across scenes and writers. Do not use for background figures who appear once; a full profile for a walk-on role is overhead. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Identity, motivation, capabilities, and limits | | | | Yes | Planned arc beats in story order | | | | No | Beat types the arc must contain | Procedure 1. Write the profile before the character acts: motivation, capability set with explicit limits, and voice rules with examples. 2. State what the character cannot do; limits are what make capability meaningful. 3. Plan the arc as an ordered beat list and check it contains the required beat types before writing. 4. Check every written scene against the profile; out-of-character action requires either a new beat that earns it or a profile revision. 5. Keep the profile versioned with the work so any scene can be traced to the character state it assumed. 6. Give each distinct character a distinguishable voice rule set; interchangeable voices are a design failure. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The recorded character profile | | | | Required arc beats not yet planned | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Out-of-character action | Scene convenience overrides the profile | Check scenes against the profile or revise it deliberately | | Missing arc stages | Key beats skipped in planning | Check required beats before writing the arc | | Interchangeable voices | All characters speak alike | Write and test a distinct voice rule per character | | Capability inflation | Limits quietly dropped under plot pressure | Restate limits in the profile and enforce them | | Stale profiles | Character grows but the record does not | Version the profile with each earned change | Security and Authority Boundary Characters borrowed from real people or cultures carry real obligations. Design with researched respect, avoid caricature, and keep provenance notes so borrowed elements are used with attribution and consent where applicable. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of characterization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characterization). 2. Wikipedia’s overview of the character arc (https://en. wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_arc). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. {
    "id": "13-creative/color-palette-generation",
    "title": "Color Palette Generation",
    "category": "13-creative",
    "level": "basic",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Generate color palettes with grounded color theory, checking contrast ratios, accessibility thresholds, and perceptual harmony so palettes work for real interfaces, not just swatches.",
    "body": "Color Palette Generation Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A palette is a system of roles with constraints, not a set of attractive colors. The skill covers deriving palettes from a base hue using declared harmony strategies, assigning roles such as background, surface, text, accent, and state, then verifying the assignments against WCAG contrast thresholds and the expected display contexts. A palette ships only with its measured contrast table, because the ratios are the part that makes it usable. When to Use Use when an interface, brand, or document needs a coherent set of colors with known contrast behavior across text, states, and backgrounds. Do not judge a palette by its swatches alone. Colors that look harmonious side by side can fail legibility the moment one becomes text on another. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Anchor color as a hex value or named reference | | | | No | Harmony rule: (default), , , or | | | | No | Required palette roles; defaults to interface roles | Procedure 1. Convert the base color to a working space such as HSL or OKLCH and derive candidate steps. 2. Generate harmony candidates per the chosen strategy, keeping lightness and saturation controlled. 3. Assign roles: background, surface, text, accent, and state colors. 4. Compute contrast ratios for every text-on-background pairing the design needs. 5. Adjust lightness until all required pairings pa ss WCAG AA, or better where the brief demands. 6. Emit the palette with hex values, roles, and the measured contrast table. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Colors with hex values and assigned roles | | | | Measured ratio for each required pairing | | | | Pass or fail per pairing against the stated threshold | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Illegible text pairs | Palette judged visually without measurement | Compute and enforce WCAG ratios for all pairs | | Vibrancy-only harmony | All steps share similar lightness | Spread lightness across roles deliberately | | Context-blind colors | Palette tuned for one background only | Verify pairings on every expected background | | State colors ambiguous | Error, warning, and success hues too close | Separate state hues and test with color-vision simulation | | Swatch-to-system mismatch | Colors unassigned to roles | Always emit roles with values | Security and Authority Boundary Palettes carry accessibility obligations in many products. Do not soften measured thresholds to save an aesthetic, and test with color-vision deficiency simulation before shipping state colors that users must distinguish to operate safely. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Adobe Color harmony and accessibility tool (https://color.adobe.com/). 2. The Wikipedia article on color theory (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_theory). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "description": "Write character dialogue with explicit speaker turns, subtext layers, and mechanical exchange checks so conversations stay consistent, purposeful, and attributable line by line.",
    "body": "Dialogue Writing Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Dialogue has mechanics and meaning: every line belongs to a speaker, turns should not blur into monologue by accident, and what a character says should rarely be exactly what they mean. This skill treats dialogue as structured data — (speaker, text) turns with optional subtext — plus checks for alternation, tagging, and emptiness, so the craft decisions sit on a verifiable exchange structure. When to Use Use when writing scenes of two or more voices where speaker attribution and turn structure must stay clean — prose, scripts, or interactive fiction. Do not use for interior monologue; unattributed thought is not dialogue and follows different rules. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Dialogue turns in order with explicit speakers | | | | No | Intended unstated meaning per line | | | | No | Per-speaker voice constraints | Procedure 1. Write every line as an explicit (speaker, text) turn; unattributed lines are a structural defect, not a style. 2. Run the exchange checks before polishing prose: same-speaker runs must be intentional, empty lines removed. 3. Give each line a purpose — information, pressure, or relationship change — and cut lines with none. 4. Set the subtext deliberately; when text equals meaning, that sameness should be the decision, not the default. 5. Read voices against their speaker rules; a line that fits no voice is a draf t error. 6. Keep the exchange table with the draft so revisions do not silently drop speakers or turns. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The checked, ordered exchange | | | | Structural problems found by the checks | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Speaker blur | Turns run together without clear attribution | Tag every line and run the alternation check | | Talking heads | Exchange carries no scene purpose | Give each line information, pressure, or change | | Flat text | Characters say exactly what they mean | Set subtext deliberately per line | | Voice bleed | All characters speak with one voice | Write per-speaker voice rules and check against them | | Unversioned drafts | Revisions drop turns silently | Keep the exchange table with the draft | Security and Authority Boundary Dialogue written in real people’s voices — impressions of living individuals — carries defamation and dignity risks. Fictional voices should stay fictional, and borrowed real-world dialect deserves researched respect. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1.
